prompt:
Write an opinion piece of about 800 words on whether cities should remove minimum parking requirements from their planning rules. Take a side and argue for it.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists. Let the length of each sentence follow what it has to say. Do not use a short sentence to set up a longer one.
context_note: Prompt sent as the subagent's whole task. The subagent also carried the Claude Code agent system prompt, tool definitions and CLAUDE.md.

text:
Every city that requires a developer to build a fixed number of parking spaces per apartment, per hundred square meters of retail, or per restaurant seat is making a bet that it can predict, years in advance and block by block, how much parking private actors will want to provide, and the evidence from the places that have tested that bet is that the city almost always guesses wrong, and wrong in a direction that costs ordinary residents real money. Cities should repeal minimum parking requirements entirely, and they should do it not because cars are bad or because parking never matters, but because the minimums substitute a blunt formula for decisions that owners, lenders, and tenants are better placed to make.

Consider where the numbers come from. Most municipal codes trace back to the Institute of Transportation Engineers' Parking Generation manual, which compiles observed peak demand at suburban sites where parking was free and abundant, often from a handful of surveys, and a planner who copies those figures into an ordinance has converted a description of what people did when parking cost them nothing into a rule about what everyone must build. Donald Shoup documented this in The High Cost of Free Parking, and the problem has not gone away: a required ratio that is correct for a freestanding pharmacy off a highway is wrong for a corner shop in a walkable neighborhood, and it is wrong again for a building beside a rail station, yet the code applies it anyway because exceptions require hearings, variances, and the patience of a lawyer.

The cost of that error lands on housing. A structured parking space commonly costs tens of thousands of dollars to build, and an underground space in an expensive metro can cost several times that, and because the requirement forces the space to be built whether or not the buyer or renter wants it, the expense is bundled into the rent or the sale price. A household without a car pays for a space it will never use, which makes the rule a transfer from the poorest households, who own the fewest vehicles, to the households that own the most. Developers respond by dropping units, since every parking stall consumes land and floor area that could have held an apartment, and on small urban lots the requirement can make a project impossible, which means the missing homes are never built at all and nobody sees what was lost.

Defenders reply that without minimums, developers will under-supply parking and spill cars onto neighborhood streets, and the worry deserves a serious answer rather than a dismissal. The answer is that spillover is a problem of how curb space is priced, and a minimum requirement addresses it the way a ration card addresses a shortage of bread, by forcing production while leaving the underlying price at zero. If a residential street fills up because the curb is free, the remedy is a permit program or a metered rate that rises until a space or two is open on every block, and that remedy produces revenue that cities can spend on the street itself. Buffalo eliminated its citywide minimums in 2017, and Minneapolis, Austin, and a growing number of other cities have followed, and the sky has not fallen in any of them; what changed is that builders began choosing their own parking levels, and many chose to provide plenty, because lenders and buyers still value a space where cars are needed.

That last point is the one critics tend to miss. Removing a mandate does not ban parking. It returns the decision to someone with a stake in getting it right, and the market is far from hostile to parking: suburban developers will keep building generously because their customers drive everywhere, while a developer downtown can build exactly what the site supports. Parking lots do not vanish; they simply stop being compulsory, which is a different thing, and one that lets a church share its lot with the apartment next door, lets a bakery open in an old storefront without a variance, and lets an owner convert a half-empty garage into homes.

There is also a plain fiscal argument. Land set aside for surface parking pays little in property tax compared with the same land holding buildings, so a city that mandates asphalt is choosing the least productive use of its most valuable ground and then wondering why its downtown looks hollow after five o'clock. Mandated lots also push destinations apart, which makes walking and transit impractical and pushes more trips into cars, so the rule produces the very demand for parking that it claims merely to be meeting, in a loop that planners rarely admit to.

None of this requires cities to be hostile to drivers. Cities can still regulate the design of garages and lots, can still set maximums where they have good reason to, and can still price curbs sensibly. What they should stop doing is dictating a number of spaces before anyone has even asked who the building is for. A rule that raises the price of housing, wastes valuable land, and rests on data gathered at suburban pharmacies has no business surviving a modern planning review, and the cities that have repealed it have shown that the cost of letting go is small while the gains compound every time someone builds something the old code would have forbidden.
